Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a quick, step‑by‑step checklist you can run locally to **(1) make sure the file is a valid PMTiles archive, (2) see the zoom range and bounds, and (3) list every vector (or raster) layer that lives inside it**.  
All of the commands use the official **PMTiles CLI** – a single binary that works on macOS, Linux and Windows (or via Docker). No server is needed.

---

## 1️⃣ Install the PMTiles CLI (if you haven’t already)

| OS | Command |
|----|---------|
| macOS (brew) | `brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles` |
| Linux (deb/ rpm) | Download the appropriate binary from the [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases) and put it on your `$PATH`. |
| Windows | Grab `pmtiles-windows-amd64.exe`, rename to `pmtiles.exe`, and add its folder to `PATH`. |
| Docker (any OS) | `docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/data protomaps/go-pmtiles:latest <subcommand> …` (replace `<subcommand>` with the commands below). |

> **Tip:** The CLI is a single static binary – no Node, Java, or Python runtime is required.

---

## 2️⃣ Verify the archive is structurally sound

```bash
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles
```

*What you’ll see*

```
✔︎ Header checksum OK
✔︎ Tile index checksum OK
✔︎ Tile data checksum OK
✔︎ No overlapping tile ranges
✔︎ File size matches header
```

If any line is red or ends with `FAIL`, the file is corrupted (e.g. an incomplete upload, a bad conversion). In that case:

* Re‑run the conversion (`pmtiles convert …`) or the tile generator (tippecanoe/planetiler) and make sure the process finishes without error.
* If you used `pmtiles extract` to cut a subset, run `pmtiles verify` on the **original** file first – a bad source will propagate.

---

## 3️⃣ Show the archive’s header & TileJSON

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
```

Typical output (truncated for brevity):

```
File: mydata.pmtiles
Version: 2
Tile type: vector
Bounds: -180.0,-85.0511,180.0,85.0511
Zoom range: 0‑14
Tile count: 1 234 567
Tile compression: gzip
Metadata:
  name = "My custom basemap"
  description = "Vector tiles for the city of X"
  attribution = "© OpenStreetMap contributors"
  format = "pbf"
```

*Why this matters*

* **`Zoom range`** tells you the min/max zoom that the archive actually contains. MapLibre will automatically over‑zoom beyond `maxzoom` if you reference the source with `url:` (not `tiles:`).  
* **`Bounds`** let you know the geographic extent – useful for splitting a huge global file into regional extracts later.  
* **`Metadata`** is where many tools store the list of layer names (see next step). If you don’t see a `layers=` entry, you can still discover them programmatically.

---

## 4️⃣ List the vector (or raster) layers inside the file

### 4.1 Quick‑look with `pmtiles show` (most recent CLI)

The latest CLI prints a `layers=` line when the archive contains a **TileJSON** block (most generators do). Example:

```
layers = water,landuse,roads,buildings,places
```

If you see that line you’re done – those are the exact `source-layer` names you’ll use in your MapLibre style.

### 4.2 When `layers=` is missing (e.g. a raw MBTiles‑to‑PMTiles conversion)

You can ask the CLI to dump the **TileJSON** that the protocol handler would return:

```bash
pmtiles tilejson mydata.pmtiles
```

Output (pretty‑printed JSON):

```json
{
  "tilejson": "2.2.0",
  "name": "My custom basemap",
  "bounds": [-180,-85.0511,180,85.0511],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "vector_layers": [
    {"id":"water","description":"Water bodies"},
    {"id":"landuse","description":"Land use polygons"},
    {"id":"roads","description":"Road network"},
    {"id":"buildings","description":"Building footprints"},
    {"id":"places","description":"Cities, towns, villages"}
  ]
}
```

The `vector_layers` array is the authoritative source‑layer list. For raster archives you’ll see `"raster_layers"` instead.

### 4.3 Programmatic inspection (Node / browser)

If you already have a small script in your project, you can use the **pmtiles JavaScript library** to read the header without uploading:

```js
import { PMTiles } from "pmtiles";
import fs from "fs";

(async () => {
  const data = fs.readFileSync("mydata.pmtiles");
  const archive = await PMTiles.fromArrayBuffer(data.buffer);
  const header = await archive.getHeader();
  console.log("Zoom range:", header.minZoom, "-", header.maxZoom);
  console.log("Layers:", header.metadata?.vector_layers?.map(l => l.id));
})();
```

Running this prints the same layer list you’d get from `pmtiles tilejson`. It’s handy when you’re already in a Node environment (e.g. a CI step that validates a newly‑generated file before you push it to S3).

---

## 5️⃣ (Optional) Extract a smaller test file to sanity‑check rendering

If the archive is huge (hundreds of MB) and you want a quick local test, you can cut a tiny bounding‑box slice:

```bash
pmtiles extract \
  --bbox=-0.15,51.5,-0.10,51.55 \   # London centre (lon1,lat1,lon2,lat2)
  --minzoom=12 --maxzoom=14 \
  mydata.pmtiles london-test.pmtiles
```

Then run `pmtiles verify` and `pmtiles show` on `london-test.pmtiles`. You can even spin up a tiny static server (`python -m http.server 8000`) and point a local MapLibre map at `pmtiles://http://localhost:8000/london-test.pmtiles` to confirm the layer names work before you upload the full file.

---

## 6️⃣ Checklist before you upload

| ✅ Item | How to confirm |
|--------|----------------|
| **File is not corrupted** | `pmtiles verify` returns all ✔︎ |
| **Zoom range matches what you expect** | `pmtiles show` → `Zoom range:` |
| **Geographic bounds are correct** | `pmtiles show` → `Bounds:` |
| **Layer list is known** | `pmtiles show` (or `pmtiles tilejson`) → `layers=` or `vector_layers` |
| **Metadata includes required attribution** | Look for `attribution` in the `Metadata:` block (OSM data → “© OpenStreetMap contributors”). |
| **CORS & Range support on the host** | After upload, run `curl -I -H "Range: bytes=0-0" https://…/mydata.pmtiles` – you should see `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). |
| **Cache‑control header** | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000` (or another long max‑age) so CDNs cache the file. |

If any of the above fails, fix it locally, re‑run the steps, and only then push the file to S3 / R2 / GitHub Pages.

---

## 7️⃣ Quick “one‑liner” for CI pipelines

You can embed the verification in a CI job (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.):

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pmtiles.yml
name: Validate PMTiles
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install pmtiles CLI
        run: |
          curl -L -o pmtiles https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64
          chmod +x pmtiles
          sudo mv pmtiles /usr/local/bin/
      - name: Verify archive
        run: |
          pmtiles verify ./tiles/mydata.pmtiles
          pmtiles show ./tiles/mydata.pmtiles > /tmp/pmtiles-info.txt
          grep -q "layers =" /tmp/pmtiles-info.txt || (echo "❌ No layer list found!" && exit 1)
```

If the job passes, you can safely publish the artifact.

---

## TL;DR – The exact commands you need

```bash
# 1️⃣ Verify integrity
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles

# 2️⃣ Show header / TileJSON (includes bounds, zooms, metadata)
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles

# 3️⃣ Get the explicit layer list (most reliable)
pmtiles tilejson mydata.pmtiles   # → look at "vector_layers" or "layers"
#   or, if you have a recent CLI:
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles | grep layers
```

Once you see the `layers = …` line (or the `vector_layers` array) and the verify step reports all ✔︎, you’re ready to upload the file to any static host that supports **HTTP Range** and **CORS** (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, Netlify, etc.). After upload, just add the protocol handler in your MapLibre app:

```js
import * as pmtiles from "pmtiles";
import maplibregl from "maplibre-gl";

const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
maplibregl.addProtocol("pmtiles", protocol.tile);   // one‑time global registration

// style example (vector)
const style = {
  version: 8,
  sources: {
    mytiles: {
      type: "vector",
      url: "pmtiles://https://my.cdn.com/mydata.pmtiles"
    }
  },
  layers: [
    { id: "water", type: "fill", source: "mytiles", "source-layer": "water", paint: { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } },
    // …other layers using the same source
  ]
};
```

That’s it – you now know exactly **what’s inside** the PMTiles file, that it’s **valid**, and you can safely push it to a static bucket and use it in MapLibre without a tile server. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR  
You used a **`tiles:`** array (`pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}`) instead of a **`url:`** property.  
When MapLibre reads a `tiles:` source it **does not look inside the PMTiles archive** for the min‑/max‑zoom values that are stored in the file header.  
So the style falls back to the default `maxzoom: 22`.  
At zoom levels that are **higher than the archive actually contains**, the protocol still tries to fetch a tile, the range request returns an empty byte‑range, and MapLibre draws a blank tile.

Switch to `url:` (or explicitly set `minzoom`/`maxzoom` yourself) and the problem disappears.

---

## What’s happening under the hood

| Property | What MapLibre does | What the PMTiles protocol does |
|----------|-------------------|--------------------------------|
| `url: "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles"` | Calls the **PMTiles protocol handler**. The handler opens the archive, reads its **header**, and returns a **TileJSON** that contains the correct `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, etc. When a tile request is made, the handler issues an HTTP **Range** request for the exact byte slice that holds that tile. | The handler knows the real zoom range (e.g. 0‑14). If you ask for zoom 15 it will **over‑zoom** using the highest‑available tiles, just like a normal vector source. |
| `tiles: ["pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"]` | Treats the source as a *template URL* and **does not read the archive header**. It therefore assumes the default `minzoom: 0, maxzoom: 22`. The TileJSON it builds has no knowledge of the archive’s limits. | The protocol still receives the same URL, but because MapLibre thinks the source supports zoom 22 it will request tiles that simply do not exist in the file. The range request returns an empty response → blank tile. |

### Why the blank tiles appear only *after* a certain zoom

- Up to the archive’s native `maxzoom` (e.g. 14) the range request finds a tile → it renders correctly.
- At `z = maxzoom + 1` (15) the client asks for a tile that isn’t stored. The PMTiles file returns **zero bytes** for that range, which MapLibre interprets as “no data” → the vector layer draws nothing (or a raster layer shows a transparent tile).
- Because the style still thinks the source can go to 22, the client keeps requesting higher zooms, all of which are empty.

---

## How to fix it

### 1. Use the `url:` property (recommended)

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "myPmtiles": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "water",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "myPmtiles",
      "source-layer": "water",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
    }
    // …other layers…
  ]
}
```

- The PMTiles library reads the header, injects the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, and over‑zooms automatically.
- No extra configuration needed.

### 2. If you *must* use a `tiles:` array (rare)

Add the correct zoom limits yourself:

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14   // <-- match the archive’s maxzoom
}
```

- This tells MapLibre not to request zoom levels that don’t exist.
- You still lose the automatic TileJSON metadata (bounds, attribution, etc.) that the `url:` method provides, so you’ll have to add those manually if you need them.

### 3. Verify the archive’s zoom range

```bash
pmtiles show data.pmtiles
```

You’ll see something like:

```
Header:
  minzoom: 0
  maxzoom: 14
  bounds: [-180,-85,180,85]
  tile count: 1 234 567
```

Make sure the `maxzoom` you set in the style (if you use `tiles:`) matches this value.

---

## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| **Blank tiles only at high zoom** | `tiles:` without `maxzoom` (default 22) | Switch to `url:` or set `maxzoom` manually. |
| **All tiles blank** | The host does **not** support HTTP **Range** requests or CORS headers are missing. | Ensure the static host returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). |
| **404 errors in network tab** | Using `tiles:` with a URL that the PMTiles protocol does not rewrite (e.g., missing `pmtiles://` prefix). | Keep the `pmtiles://` prefix and use the protocol handler (`maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile)`). |
| **MapLibre logs “TileJSON missing”** | You used `tiles:` but didn’t provide `minzoom`/`maxzoom`/`bounds`. | Add those properties or, better, use `url:`. |
| **Over‑zoom looks “pixelated”** | You are actually over‑zooming beyond the archive’s maxzoom. | Either generate higher‑zoom tiles or accept the over‑zoomed appearance (MapLibre will repeat the highest‑available tiles). |

---

## Quick checklist for a healthy PMTiles setup

1. **Host** – static storage that supports **Range** and **CORS**.  
   *S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages (≤100 MB), Netlify, Vercel* are all fine.
2. **Upload** – set a long `Cache‑Control` (e.g. `public, max‑age=31536000`) because the file is immutable.
3. **Register the protocol** *once* in your app (before any map is created):

   ```js
   import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles';
   import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';

   const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
   maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile);
   ```

4. **Style** – use `url:` for PMTiles sources.  
   If you must use `tiles:`, add `minzoom`/`maxzoom` that match the archive.
5. **Test** – open DevTools → Network → filter “pmtiles”.  
   You should see **Range** requests like `Range: bytes=12345-12456` returning `206 Partial Content`. No 404s, no empty bodies.

---

## TL;DR code snippet (the “right way”)

```js
import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles';
import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';
import 'maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl.css';

// 1️⃣ Register the protocol (do this once, e.g. in your app entry)
const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile);

// 2️⃣ Create the map with a PMTiles **url** source
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: {
    version: 8,
    sources: {
      world: {
        type: 'vector',
        url: 'pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles'
      }
    },
    layers: [
      {
        id: 'water',
        type: 'fill',
        source: 'world',
        'source-layer': 'water',
        paint: { 'fill-color': '#a0c8f0' }
      },
      // …more layers…
    ]
  },
  center: [0, 0],
  zoom: 2
});
```

That’s it—no blank tiles, correct zoom limits, and you get the full benefit of the PMTiles header (bounds, attribution, etc.) automatically.

---

### Gotchas after the fix

- **If you still see blanks**, double‑check the **CORS** and **Range** headers on the host. A missing `Accept-Ranges: bytes` will cause the request to return the whole file (or a 200) which MapLibre cannot parse as a single tile.
- **If you need multiple regions**, you can create several PMTiles files (e.g., `europe.pmtiles`, `asia.pmtiles`) and add them as separate sources, each with its own `url:`. Use `source-layer` to pick layers from each file.
- **Terrain (raster‑dem)** works the same way; just change the source type and add `"encoding": "terrarium"` (or `"mapbox"`).

---

**Bottom line:**  
`tiles:` bypasses the PMTiles header, so MapLibre thinks the archive supports zoom 22 and asks for tiles that don’t exist → blank tiles. Use `url:` (or manually set `maxzoom`) and the problem disappears. Happy mapping!
